draft.title: Episodic and semantic memory
card: Episodic memory holds personal events, the things that happened to you. Each one comes with a time and a place, such as your last birthday party.
Semantic memory holds general facts and knowledge about the world, such as the capital of Victoria. It does not come with the time or place you learnt it.
Both are types of long-term memory. Both are recalled on purpose, so both are explicit memories.
The two can work together. You may recall a fact (semantic) and also remember the lesson where you learnt it (episodic).
draft.remember: Episodic is your own story with a time and place. Semantic is knowing facts.

a.q: Which of these is an example of semantic memory?
opts: Knowing that water boils at 100 degrees Celsius
Remembering boiling water spill on your hand last summer
Recalling the kitchen you were in when you burnt your hand
Remembering your sister laughing when the kettle whistled
a.why: Knowing the boiling point is a general fact that is not tied to one personal moment. The other options are personal events with a time and place, so they are episodic.
a.clue: Which one is a fact anyone could know, not your own experience?

b.q: Priya sits her Year 12 exam and recalls that the Treaty of Versailles was signed in 1919. She also remembers the classroom in Ballarat where she first learnt it. Which pairing is correct?
opts: The date is semantic and the classroom memory is episodic
The date is episodic and the classroom memory is semantic
Both are semantic because both help in the exam
Both are episodic because both were learnt at school
b.why: The date is a general fact, so it is semantic. Remembering the classroom is a personal experience with a place, so it is episodic. Where a fact was learnt does not make the fact itself episodic.
b.clue: Sort the fact from the personal experience of learning it.

a.best: Knowing that water boils at 100 degrees Celsius

b.best: The date is semantic and the classroom memory is episodic
